items.bewering: Die eerste boere het graan geplant en vee aangehou
items.bron: SA History Online, 'When, why and where the first African farmers settled in southern Africa' (sahistory.org.za): the farmers grew sorghum and kept cattle, sheep and goats. Jones et al. 2023, Journal of Archaeological Research (s10814-023-09194-y), and the University of Pretoria repository: Early Iron Age farmers grew millet and sorghum (both grains) and kept livestock. 'Eerste boere' follows the established South African usage, where 'first farmers' means these Early Iron Age agropastoralists (from c. AD 200-300). Khoekhoe herders with sheep arrived earlier but planted no crops and are called herders, not farmers, in this usage. So the superlative holds within its convention. The same phrase in 'Twee soorte genesers' is covered by this item.

items.bewering: maar hulle het steeds wild gejag.
items.bron: Jones et al. 2023, 'Hunting and the social lives of Southern Africa's first farmers', Journal of Archaeological Research (abstract via ora.ox.ac.uk): a study of 54 Iron Age sites finds that hunting characterised the spread of farming in southern Africa. SA History Online: 'The men still hunted, but also herded cattle, goats and sheep.'

items.bewering: Hulle het bokke en hase gejag
items.bron: Voigt & Peters 1994, 'The faunal assemblage from Wosi in the Thukela Valley', Natal Museum Journal of Humanities 6: 105-117 (read in full, epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/8447). This Early Iron Age farming village is dated c. AD 650-800. Its species list includes Lepus/Pronolagus (hare, NISP 9) and many antelope: blue, red and common duiker, impala, bushbuck, reedbuck, mountain reedbuck and blue wildebeest. Note: Maggs 1975 found hare rare or absent at southern Highveld sites (later Iron Age), so hares were a minor prey, but the claim does not say otherwise.

items.bewering: vir die vleis en ook vir die velle en bene.
items.bron: Meat: wild bovids in the Wosi middens (Voigt & Peters 1994). Skins: the same report says wild felids at Wosi were 'possibly hunted for skins and body parts'. Bones: a microwear study of 110 worked-bone pieces from the Early Iron Age site Broederstroom concludes the bone tools were a product of local farmer industry (Azania 59, 2024; pure.uj.ac.za). Bone hoes from the Limpopo Valley (10th-13th c.) are a further example (pure.uj.ac.za).

items.bewering: Net soos ons het die boere ook soms siek geword of seergekry.
items.bron: L'Abbé, Coetzee & Loots, 'A description of Iron Age skeletons from the Pilanesberg National Park' (repository.up.ac.za; sahris.sahra.org.za). Iron Age skeletons were examined for disease and trauma, and dental ailments such as abscesses were found.

items.bewering: Daar was nog geen apteke nie, maar die veld was vol plante.
items.bron: Pharmacies came to South Africa with the colonial period: the Pallas & Poleman record names Pallas's shop as the first apothecary shop in Cape Town (c. 1800). The farmers arrived about 1 500 years before that. Plants: over 3 000 species are used in traditional medicine in South Africa (Makunga et al. review; UNIDO Compendium of medicinal and aromatic plants, vol. 1).

items.bewering: Die boere het waarskynlik die blare, wortels en bas van medisinale plante gebruik om siek mense te behandel.
items.bron: Rests on the hedge 'waarskynlik', and the hedge is appropriate: I found no direct archaeological evidence of Early Iron Age plant medicine. Roots, bark and leaves are the plant parts used in southern African traditional medicine. SA History Online, 'Indigenous medicine and traditional healing': inyangas make medicines 'from herbs, roots and bark', with examples (bitter aloe leaves or roots, coral tree bark). Muthi-market studies (PMC8227155, PMC6500648) find roots and bark most traded and leaves used less often. All three parts named are correct.

items.bewering: Hulle het waarskynlik ook ander middels uit die natuur gebruik.
items.bron: Hedged. SA History Online, 'Indigenous medicine and traditional healing': inyangas also use ground rocks, animal horns and bones. Muthi is made from plant, animal and mineral material.

items.bewering: Die eerste boere het waarskynlik ook genesers gehad wat siek mense gehelp het.
items.bron: Hedged, and the hedge matches the evidence. Beukes, MA thesis on kwaGandaganda (core.ac.uk/download/43176373): several possible divining bones were found at this Early Iron Age site in the Mngeni valley (from AD 620). Whitelaw 1994 (Natal Museum Journal of Humanities) is the site report. 'Possible' evidence supports 'waarskynlik' and no more.

items.bewering: By latere gemeenskappe was twee soorte tradisionele genesers bekend, en dit is vandag nog so.
items.bron: SA History Online, 'Indigenous medicine and traditional healing': 'Isangomas and inyangas are the two MAIN types of indigenous or traditional healers in South Africa.' The Traditional Health Practitioners Act 22 of 2007, s. 1 (acts.co.za), registers four categories today: diviner, herbalist, traditional birth attendant and traditional surgeon. A UKZN study in northern KwaZulu-Natal also names a third type, the umthandazi (faith healer). Two kinds are the main ones, but not the only ones. The sentence says this is 'still so today', and a learner will read it as 'there are two kinds of traditional healer'. That is false for today.
items.regstelling: Narrow the quantifier and keep the rest. Say these were the two MAIN kinds of traditional healer, and still are today ('twee hoofsoorte'). The sangoma/inyanga pair stays as it is. Do not list the other categories; the narrowing is enough.

items.bewering: In isiZulu noem mense vandag die een soort geneser 'n sangoma en die ander soort 'n inyanga.
items.bron: SA History Online, 'Indigenous medicine and traditional healing'; 'Traditional healers of Southern Africa' (Wikipedia, used only for corroboration); THP Act 2007 recognises diviners (izangoma) and herbalists (izinyanga). Note, not a finding: the full isiZulu noun is isangoma (plural izangoma), and 'sangoma' is the form borrowed into Afrikaans and English. Older Zulu usage also uses inyanga for any doctor, distinguishing inyanga yokwelapha (herbalist) from inyanga yokubhula (diviner). Present-day common usage matches the lesson.

items.bewering: 'n Sangoma gee geestelike leiding. Hy of sy vra die voorouers om leiding.
items.bron: SA History Online, 'Indigenous medicine and traditional healing': sangomas are 'spiritual healers and are often women', and 'when sangomas diagnose illness, they listen to their ancestors'. 'Hy of sy' is correct: most are women, but men practise too.

items.bewering: 'n Inyanga werk met medisinale plante en weet goed watter plant om te gebruik.
items.bron: SA History Online, 'Indigenous medicine and traditional healing': inyangas are 'healers that make medicines from herbs, roots and bark', and their training is long because the wrong dose can be toxic. An inyanga is concerned mainly with medicines from plants (and animals).

items.bewering: Maar party genesers doen albei soorte werk.
items.bron: 'Traditional healers of Southern Africa': the distinction has blurred and 'traditional healers tend to practice both arts'. THP Act 2007 s. 1 (acts.co.za): a practitioner may be registered 'in one or more of the categories'.

items.bewering: Die boere het nie opgeskryf wat hulle van plante geweet het nie.
items.bron: Jeff Guy, 'First farmers' (SA History Online archive): the period of roughly 2000 to 1000 years ago is too remote for oral tradition to help, and 'there are no written records'. Knowledge of the first farmers depends on archaeology.

items.bewering: Ouer mense het waarskynlik jonger mense gewys watter plante om te soek en hoe om hulle te gebruik. So kon die kennis van geslag tot geslag oorgedra word.
items.bron: Hedged, and well supported as a mechanism. SA History Online, 'Indigenous medicine and traditional healing': in the past an inyanga chose a promising child, who was 'taught which plants and herbs to use for healing'. THP Act 2007 s. 1 defines 'traditional philosophy' as indigenous knowledge passed from ancestors to descendants, with or without written records. Herbalists still learn by apprenticeship (UCT humanities source).

items.bewering: Op dié manier het genesers honderde jare lank siek mense bly help.
items.bron: 'Hundreds of years' is a modest span. Izinyanga and izangoma are described in 19th- and early 20th-century Zulu ethnography, which already gives about two centuries. There are possible divining bones at Early Iron Age kwaGandaganda (7th century AD; Beukes thesis). The claim does not exceed the evidence.

items.bewering: Daar is vandag nog steeds tradisionele genesers wat in Suid-Afrika werk.
items.bron: Traditional Health Practitioners Act 22 of 2007 (gov.za, acts.co.za) and the Department of Health's notice 'Efforts to strengthen and promote traditional medicine' (gov.za, 2015). Registration under the Act began in 2016. I give no headcount: the often-quoted 200 000 is disputed (NWU repository), and the lesson wisely gives no number.

items.bewering: geneser: Iemand wat siek of seer mense behandel om hulle gesond te maak.
items.bron: Read on its own. A healer (geneser) is one who treats the sick or injured to restore health. This matches the THP Act's description of traditional health practice ('to maintain or restore health ... diagnose, treat or prevent illness', acts.co.za s. 1) and the general sense of the word. Not limited to traditional healers, which is correct for a general term.

items.bewering: sangoma: Die isiZulu-woord vir 'n geneser wat die voorouers om leiding vra.
items.bron: Read on its own. SA History Online: sangomas diagnose by listening to the ancestors. The word comes from isiZulu (isangoma). See the note on the isiZulu prefix under the block 'Twee soorte genesers'; it is not a fault at this level.

items.bewering: inyanga: Die isiZulu-woord vir 'n geneser wat met medisinale plante werk.
items.bron: Read on its own. SA History Online: inyangas make medicines from herbs, roots and bark. In current isiZulu and South African usage inyanga is the herbalist.

items.bewering: medisinale plant: 'n Plant waarvan mense dele gebruik om siektes te behandel.
items.bron: Read on its own. Consistent with the usage in the sources above (plants whose roots, bark, leaves or bulbs are used in remedies; muthi-market studies PMC8227155, PMC6500648).

items.bewering: voorouers: Die mense in jou familie van wie jy afstam en wat reeds oorlede is, soos 'n ouma of oupa wat al gesterf het.
items.bron: Read on its own. Afrikaans voorouer = ancestor, from Dutch voorouder: the people of one's line who lived before and from whom one descends (Wiktionary; older Dutch dictionary at dbnl.org). In the isiZulu tradition the lesson draws on, the amadlozi are the family's departed elders who watch over their descendants (South African Tourism, 'African ancestors and amadlozi', southafrica.net). Deceased grandparents fall squarely inside both senses, so the example holds.

items.bewering: bas: Die harde buitenste laag van 'n boom se stam en takke.
items.bron: Read on its own. 'Bark (botany)' and Britannica 'bark (plant tissue)': bark is the outermost layer of the stems and roots of woody plants, popularly all tissue outside the wood. NYBG glossary: tissue of trunk and branches outside the cambium. 'Harde' describes the protective outer bark and is an everyday simplification, not universal: the inner bark is living and soft. It does not mislead at this level or in this lesson.

opsomming: Every claim checks out against sources except one: the lesson says there were two kinds of traditional healer and 'it is still so today', but sources call the sangoma and inyanga the two MAIN kinds, and South African law today registers four categories, so the writer should narrow this to 'twee hoofsoorte' and change nothing else.
